John Bartlett (1820–1905).  Familiar Quotations, 10th ed.  1919.

William Wordsworth 1770-1850 John Bartlett

 

1
    Oh, be wiser thou!
Instructed that true knowledge leads to love.

          
Lines left upon a Seat in a Yew-tree
.

2
    And homeless near a thousand homes I stood,
And near a thousand tables pined and wanted food.

          
Guilt and Sorrow
. Stanza 41.

3
    Action is transitory,—a step, a blow;
The motion of a muscle, this way or that.

          
The Borderers
. Act iii.

4
    Three sleepless nights I passed in sounding on,
Through words and things, a dim and perilous way.
 
1

          
The Borderers
. Act iv. Sc. 2.

5
    A simple child
That lightly draws its breath,
And feels its life in every limb,
What should it know of death?

          
We are Seven
.

6
    O Reader! had you in your mind
Such stores as silent thought can bring,
O gentle Reader! you would find
A tale in everything.

          
Simon Lee
.

7
    I ’ve heard of hearts unkind, kind deeds
With coldness still returning;
Alas! the gratitude of men
Hath oftener left me mourning.

          
Simon Lee
.

8
    In that sweet mood when pleasant thoughts
Bring sad thoughts to the mind.

          
Lines written in Early Spring
.

9
    And ’t is my faith, that every flower
Enjoys the air it breathes.

          
Lines written in Early Spring
.

10
    Nor less I deem that there are Powers
Which of themselves our minds impress;
That we can feed this mind of ours
In a wise passiveness.

          
Expostulation and Reply
.

  

  

  

11
    Up! up! my friend, and quit your books,
Or surely you ’ll grow double!
Up! up! my friend, and clear your looks!
Why all this toil and trouble?

          
The Tables Turned
.

12
    Come forth into the light of things,
Let Nature be your teacher.

          
The Tables Turned
.

13
    One impulse from a vernal wood
May teach you more of man,
Of moral evil and of good,
Than all the sages can.

          
The Tables Turned
.

14
    The bane of all that dread the Devil.

          
The Idiot Boy
.

15
    Sensations sweet,
Felt in the blood, and felt along the heart.

          
Lines completed a few miles above Tintern Abbey
.

16
    That best portion of a good man’s life,—
His little, nameless, unremembered acts
Of kindness and of love.

          
Lines completed a few miles above Tintern Abbey
.

17
    That blessed mood,
In which the burden of the mystery,
In which the heavy and the weary weight
Of all this unintelligible world,
Is lightened.

          
Lines completed a few miles above Tintern Abbey
.

18
    The fretful stir
Unprofitable, and the fever of the world
Have hung upon the beatings of my heart.

          
Lines completed a few miles above Tintern Abbey
.

19
    The sounding cataract
Haunted me like a passion; the tall rock,
The mountain, and the deep and gloomy wood,
Their colours and their forms, were then to me
An appetite,—a feeling and a love,
That had no need of a remoter charm
By thoughts supplied, nor any interest
Unborrowed from the eye.

          
Lines completed a few miles above Tintern Abbey
.

20
    But hearing oftentimes
The still, sad music of humanity.

          
Lines completed a few miles above Tintern Abbey
.

21
    A sense sublime
Of something far more deeply interfused,
Whose dwelling is the light of setting suns,
And the round ocean and the living air
And the blue sky, and in the mind of man,—
A motion and a spirit, that impels
All thinking things, all objects of all thought,
And rolls through all things.

          
Lines completed a few miles above Tintern Abbey
.

22
    Knowing that Nature never did betray
The heart that loved her.

          
Lines completed a few miles above Tintern Abbey
.

23
    Nor greetings where no kindness is, nor all
The dreary intercourse of daily life.

          
Lines completed a few miles above Tintern Abbey
.

24
    Men who can hear the Decalogue, and feel
To self-reproach.

          
The Old Cumberland Beggar
.

25
    As in the eye of Nature he has lived,
So in the eye of Nature let him die!

          
The Old Cumberland Beggar
.

26
    There ’s something in a flying horse,
There ’s something in a huge balloon.

          
Peter Bell
. Prologue. Stanza 1.

27
    The common growth of Mother Earth
Suffices me,—her tears, her mirth,
Her humblest mirth and tears.

          
Peter Bell
. Prologue. Stanza 27.

28
    Full twenty times was Peter feared,
For once that Peter was respected.

          
Peter Bell
. Part i. Stanza 3.

29
    A primrose by a river’s brim
A yellow primrose was to him,
And it was nothing more.

          
Peter Bell
. Part i. Stanza 12.

30
    The soft blue sky did never melt
Into his heart; he never felt
The witchery of the soft blue sky!

          
Peter Bell
. Part i. Stanza 15.

31
    On a fair prospect some have looked,
And felt, as I have heard them say,
As if the moving time had been
A thing as steadfast as the scene
On which they gazed themselves away.

          
Peter Bell
. Part i. Stanza 16.

32
    As if the man had fixed his face,
In many a solitary place,
Against the wind and open sky!

          
Peter Bell
. Part i. Stanza 16.
 
 
2

33
    One of those heavenly days that cannot die.

          
Nutting
.

34
    She dwelt among the untrodden ways
  Beside the springs of Dove,—
A maid whom there were none to praise
  And very few to love.

          
She dwelt among the untrodden ways
.

35
    A violet by a mossy stone
  Half hidden from the eye;
Fair as a star, when only one
  Is shining in the sky.

          
She dwelt among the untrodden ways
.

36
    She lived unknown, and few could know
  When Lucy ceased to be;
But she is in her grave, and oh
  The difference to me!

          
She dwelt among the untrodden ways
.

37
    The stars of midnight shall be dear
To her; and she shall lean her ear
  In many a secret place
Where rivulets dance their wayward round,
And beauty born of murmuring sound
  Shall pass into her face.

          
Three years she grew in Sun and Shower
.

38
    May no rude hand deface it,
And its forlorn 
hic jacet!

          
Ellen Irwin
.

39
    She gave me eyes, she gave me ears;
And humble cares, and delicate fears;
A heart, the fountain of sweet tears;
  And love and thought and joy.

          
The Sparrow’s Nest
.

40
    The child is father of the man.
 
3

          
My heart leaps up when I behold
.

41
        The cattle are grazing,
    Their heads never raising;
There are forty feeding like one!

          
The Cock is crowing.

42
    Sweet childish days, that were as long
As twenty days are now.

          
To a Butterfly
. I ’ve watched you now a full half-hour.

43
    Often have I sighed to measure
By myself a lonely pleasure,—
Sighed to think I read a book,
Only read, perhaps, by me.

          
To the Small Celandine
.

44
    As high as we have mounted in delight,
In our dejection do we sink as low.

          
Resolution and Independence
. Stanza 4.

45
    But how can he expect that others should
Build for him, sow for him, and at his call
Love him, who for himself will take no heed at all?

          
Resolution and Independence
. Stanza 6.

46
    I thought of Chatterton, the marvellous boy,
The sleepless soul that perished in his pride;
Of him who walked in glory and in joy,
Following his plough, along the mountain-side.
By our own spirits we are deified;
We Poets in our youth begin in gladness,
But thereof come in the end despondency and madness.

          
Resolution and Independence
. Stanza 7.

47
    That heareth not the loud winds when they call,
And moveth all together, if it moves at all.

          
Resolution and Independence
. Stanza 11.

48
    Choice word and measured phrase above the reach
Of ordinary men.

          
Resolution and Independence
. Stanza 14.

49
    And mighty poets in their misery dead.

          
Resolution and Independence
. Stanza 17.

50
    Ne’er saw I, never felt, a calm so deep!
The river glideth at his own sweet will;
Dear God! the very houses seem asleep;
And all that mighty heart is lying still!

          
Earth has not anything to show more fair.

51
    The holy time is quiet as a nun
Breathless with adoration.

          
It is a beauteous Evening
.

52
    Men are we, and must grieve when even the shade
Of that which once was great is passed away.

          
On the Extinction of the Venetian Republic
.

53
    Thou has left behind
Powers that will work for thee,—air, earth, and skies!
There ’s not a breathing of the common wind
That will forget thee; thou hast great allies;
Thy friends are exultations, agonies,
And love, and man’s unconquerable mind.
 
4

          
To Toussaint L’Ouverture
.

54
    One that would peep and botanize
Upon his mother’s grave.

          
A Poet’s Epitaph
. Stanza 5.

55
    He murmurs near the running brooks
A music sweeter than their own.

          
A Poet’s Epitaph
. Stanza 10.

56
    And you must love him, ere to you
He will seem worthy of your love.

          
A Poet’s Epitaph
. Stanza 11.

57
    The harvest of a quiet eye,
That broods and sleeps on his own heart.

          
A Poet’s Epitaph
. Stanza 13.

58
    Yet sometimes, when the secret cup
Of still and serious thought went round,
It seemed as if he drank it up,
He felt with spirit so profound.

          
Matthew
.

59
    My eyes are dim with childish tears,
My heart is idly stirred,
For the same sound is in my ears
Which in those days I heard.

          
The Fountain
.

60
    A happy youth, and their old age
Is beautiful and free.

          
The Fountain
.

61
    And often, glad no more,
We wear a face of joy because
We have been glad of yore.

          
The Fountain
.

62
    The sweetest thing that ever grew
Beside a human door.

          
Lucy Gray
. Stanza 2.

63
        A youth to whom was given
So much of earth, so much of heaven.

          
Ruth
.

64
    Until a man might travel twelve stout miles,
Or reap an acre of his neighbor’s corn.

          
The Brothers
.

65
    Something between a hindrance and a help.

          
Michael
.

66
    Drink, pretty creature, drink!

          
The Pet Lamb
.

67
    Lady of the Mere,
Sole-sitting by the shores of old romance.

          
A narrow Girdle of rough Stones and Crags
.

68
    And he is oft the wisest man
  Who is not wise at all.

          
The Oak and the Broom
.

69
    “A jolly place,” said he, “in times of old!
But something ails it now: the spot is cursed.”

          
Hart-leap Well
. Part ii.

70
    Hunt half a day for a forgotten dream.

          
Hart-leap Well
. Part ii.

71
    Never to blend our pleasure or our pride
With sorrow of the meanest thing that feels.

          
Hart-leap Well
. Part ii.

72
    Plain living and high thinking are no more.
The homely beauty of the good old cause
Is gone; our peace, our fearful innocence,
And pure religion breathing household laws.

          
O, Friend! I know not which way I must look.

73
    Milton! thou should’st be living at this hour:
England hath need of thee!
     .     .     .     .     .     .
Thy soul was like a star, and dwelt apart:
So didst thou travel on life’s common way
In cheerful godliness.

          
London, 1802
.

74
    We must be free or die who speak the tongue
That Shakespeare spake, the faith and morals hold
Which Milton held.

          
It is not to be thought of
.

75
    A noticeable man, with large gray eyes.

          
Stanzas written in Thomson’s Castle of Indolence
.

76
    We meet thee, like a pleasant thought,
When such are wanted.

          
To the Daisy
.

77
    The poet’s darling.

          
To the Daisy
.

78
    Thou unassuming commonplace
Of Nature.

          
To the same Flower
.

79
    Oft on the dappled turf at ease
I sit, and play with similes,
Loose type of things through all degrees.

          
To the same Flower
.

80
    Sweet Mercy! to the gates of heaven
This minstrel lead, his sins forgiven;
The rueful conflict, the heart riven
  With vain endeavour,
And memory of Earth’s bitter leaven
  Effaced forever.

          
Thoughts suggested on the Banks of the Nith
.

81
    The best of what we do and are,
Just God, forgive!

          
Thoughts suggested on the Banks of the Nith
.

82
    For old, unhappy, far-off things,
And battles long ago.

          
The Solitary Reaper
.

83
    Some natural sorrow, loss, or pain
That has been, and may be again.

          
The Solitary Reaper
.

84
    The music in my heart I bore
Long after it was heard no more.

          
The Solitary Reaper
.

85
    Yon foaming flood seems motionless as ice;
Its dizzy turbulence eludes the eye,
Frozen by distance.

          
Address to Kilchurn Castle
.

86
    A famous man is Robin Hood,
The English ballad-singer’s joy.

          
Rob Roy’s Grave
.

87
        Because the good old rule
Sufficeth them,—the simple plan,
That they should take who have the power,
    And they should keep who can.

          
Rob Roy’s Grave
.

88
    The Eagle, he was lord above,
  And Rob was lord below.

          
Rob Roy’s Grave
.

89
    A brotherhood of venerable trees.

          
Sonnet composed at ———— Castle
.

90
    Let beeves and home-bred kine partake
The sweets of Burn-mill meadow;
The swan on still St. Mary’s Lake
Float double, swan and shadow!

          
Yarrow Unvisited
.

91
    Every gift of noble origin
Is breathed upon by Hope’s perpetual breath.

          
These Times strike Monied Worldlings.

92
    A remnant of uneasy light.

          
The Matron of Jedborough
.

93
    Oh for a single hour of that Dundee
Who on that day the word of onset gave!
 
5

          
Sonnet, in the Pass of Killicranky
.

94
    O Cuckoo! shall I call thee bird,
Or but a wandering voice?

          
To the Cuckoo
.

95
    She was a phantom of delight
When first she gleamed upon my sight,
A lovely apparition, sent
To be a moment’s ornament;
Her eyes as stars of twilight fair,
Like twilights too her dusky hair,
But all things else about her drawn
From May-time and the cheerful dawn.

          
She was a Phantom of Delight
.

96
    A creature not too bright or good
For human nature’s daily food;
For transient sorrows, simple wiles,
Praise, blame, love, kisses, tears, and smiles.

          
She was a Phantom of Delight
.

97
    The reason firm, the temperate will,
Endurance, foresight, strength, and skill;
A perfect woman, nobly planned,
To warn, to comfort, and command.

          
She was a Phantom of Delight
.

98
    That inward eye
Which is the bliss of solitude.

          
I wandered lonely
.

99
    To be a Prodigal’s favourite,—then, worse truth,
A Miser’s pensioner,—behold our lot!

          
The Small Celandine
.

100
    Stern Daughter of the Voice of God!
 
6

          
Ode to Duty
.

101
    A light to guide, a rod
To check the erring, and reprove.

          
Ode to Duty
.

102
    Give unto me, made lowly wise,
The spirit of self-sacrifice;
The confidence of reason give,
And in the light of truth thy bondman let me live!

          
Ode to Duty
.

103
    The light that never was, on sea or land;
The consecration, and the Poet’s dream.

          
Suggested by a Picture of Peele Castle in a Storm
. Stanza 4.

104
    Shalt show us how divine a thing
A woman may be made.

          
To a Young Lady
. Dear Child of Nature.

105
    But an old age serene and bright,
And lovely as a Lapland night,
  Shall lead thee to thy grave.

          
To a Young Lady
. Dear Child of Nature.

106
    Where the statue stood
Of Newton, with his prism and silent face,
The marble index of a mind forever
Voyaging through strange seas of thought alone.

          
The Prelude.
Book iii
.

107
    Another morn
Risen on mid-noon.
 
7

          
The Prelude.
Book vi
.

108
    Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive,
But to be young was very heaven!

          
The Prelude.
Book xi
.

109
    The budding rose above the rose full blown.

          
The Prelude.
Book xi
.

110
    There is
One great society alone on earth:
The noble living and the noble dead.

          
The Prelude.
Book xi
.

111
    Who, doomed to go in company with Pain
And Fear and Bloodshed,—miserable train!—
Turns his necessity to glorious gain.

          
Character of the Happy Warrior
.

112
    Controls them and subdues, transmutes, bereaves
Of their bad influence, and their good receives.

          
Character of the Happy Warrior
.

113
    But who, if he be called upon to face
Some awful moment to which Heaven has joined
Great issues, good or bad for humankind,
Is happy as a lover.

          
Character of the Happy Warrior
.

114
    And through the heat of conflict keeps the law
In calmness made, and sees what he foresaw.

          
Character of the Happy Warrior
.

115
    Whom neither shape of danger can dismay,
Nor thought of tender happiness betray.

          
Character of the Happy Warrior
.

116
    Like,—but oh how different!

          
Yes, it was the Mountain Echo
.

117
    The world is too much with us; late and soon,
Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers:
Little we see in Nature that is ours.

          
Miscellaneous Sonnets. Part i. xxxiii.

118
    Great God! I ’d rather be
A Pagan suckled in a creed outworn,
So might I, standing on this pleasant lea,
Have glimpses that would make me less forlorn;
Have sight of Proteus rising from the sea,
Or hear old Triton blow his wreathed horn.

          
Miscellaneous Sonnets. Part i. xxxiii.

119
    Maidens withering on the stalk.
 
8

          
Personal Talk
. Stanza 1.

120
    Sweetest melodies
Are those that are by distance made more sweet.
 
9

          
Personal Talk
. Stanza 2.

121
    Dreams, books, are each a world; and books, we know,
Are a substantial world, both pure and good.
Round these, with tendrils strong as flesh and blood,
Our pastime and our happiness will grow.

          
Personal Talk
. Stanza 3.

122
    The gentle Lady married to the Moor,
And heavenly Una with her milk-white lamb.

          
Personal Talk
. Stanza 3.

123
    Blessings be with them, and eternal praise,
Who gave us nobler loves, and nobler cares!—
The Poets, who on earth have made us heirs
Of truth and pure delight by heavenly lays.

          
Personal Talk
. Stanza 4.

124
    A power is passing from the earth.

          
Lines on the expected Dissolution of Mr. Fox.

125
    The rainbow comes and goes,
And lovely is the rose.

          
Intimations of Immortality
. Stanza 2.

126
        The sunshine is a glorious birth;
    But yet I know, where’er I go,
That there hath passed away a glory from the earth.

          
Intimations of Immortality
. Stanza 2.

127
    Where is it now, the glory and the dream?

          
Intimations of Immortality
. Stanza 5.

128
    Our birth is but a sleep and a forgetting:
The soul that rises with us, our life’s star,
    Hath had elsewhere its setting,
      And cometh from afar.
    Not in entire forgetfulness,
    And not in utter nakedness,
But trailing clouds of glory, do we come
    From God, who is our home:
Heaven lies about us in our infancy.

          
Intimations of Immortality
. Stanza 5.

129
    At length the man perceives it die away,
And fade into the light of common day.

          
Intimations of Immortality
. Stanza 5.

130
    The thought of our past years in me doth breed
Perpetual benediction.

          
Intimations of Immortality
. Stanza 9.

131
              Those obstinate questionings
    Of sense and outward things,
    Fallings from us, vanishings,
    Blank misgivings of a creature
Moving about in worlds not realized,
High instincts before which our mortal nature
Did tremble like a guilty thing surprised.

          
Intimations of Immortality
. Stanza 9.

132
    Truths that wake,
To perish never.

          
Intimations of Immortality
. Stanza 9.

133
        Though inland far we be,
Our souls have sight of that immortal sea
    Which brought us hither.

          
Intimations of Immortality
. Stanza 9.

134
    Though nothing can bring back the hour
Of splendour in the grass, of glory in the flower.

          
Intimations of Immortality
. Stanza 10.

135
    In years that bring the philosophic mind.

          
Intimations of Immortality
. Stanza 10.

136
    The clouds that gather round the setting sun
Do take a sober colouring from an eye
That hath kept watch o’er man’s mortality.

          
Intimations of Immortality
. Stanza 11.

137
    To me the meanest flower that blows can give
Thoughts that do often lie too deep for tears.

          
Intimations of Immortality
. Stanza 11.

138
    Two voices are there: one is of the sea,
One of the mountains,—each a mighty voice.

          
Thought of a Briton on the Subjugation of Switzerland
.

139
    Earth helped him with the cry of blood.
 
10

          
Song at the Feast of Broughton Castle
.

140
    The silence that is in the starry sky.

          Ibid.

141
    The monumental pomp of age
Was with this goodly personage;
A stature undepressed in size,
Unbent, which rather seemed to rise
In open victory o’er the weight
Of seventy years, to loftier height.

          
The White Doe of Rylstone
. Canto iii.

142
    “What is good for a bootless bene?”
With these dark words begins my tale;
And their meaning is, Whence can comfort spring
When prayer is of no avail?

          
Force of Prayer
.

143
    A few strong instincts, and a few plain rules.

          
Alas! what boots the long laborious Quest
?

144
    Of blessed consolations in distress.

          
Preface to the Excursion
.
 (Edition, 1814.)

145
    The vision and the faculty divine;
Yet wanting the accomplishment of verse.

          
The Excursion.
Book i
.

146
    The imperfect offices of prayer and praise.

          
The Excursion.
Book i
.

147
    That mighty orb of song,
The divine Milton.

          
The Excursion.
Book i
.

148
    The good die first,
 
11
And they whose hearts are dry as summer dust
Burn to the socket.

          
The Excursion.
Book i
.

149
    This dull product of a scoffer’s pen.

          
The Excursion.
Book ii
.

150
    With battlements that on their restless fronts
Bore stars.

          
The Excursion.
Book ii
.

151
    Wisdom is ofttimes nearer when we stoop
Than when we soar.

          
The Excursion.
Book iii
.

152
    Wrongs unredressed, or insults unavenged.

          
The Excursion.
Book iii
.

153
    Monastic brotherhood, upon rock
Aerial.

          
The Excursion.
Book iii
.

154
    The intellectual power, through words and things,
Went sounding on a dim and perilous way!
 
12

          
The Excursion.
Book iii
.

155
    Society became my glittering bride,
And airy hopes my children.

          
The Excursion.
Book iii
.

156
    And the most difficult of tasks to keep
Heights which the soul is competent to gain.

          
The Excursion.
Book iv
.

157
    There is a luxury in self-dispraise;
And inward self-disparagement affords
To meditative spleen a grateful feast.

          
The Excursion.
Book iv
.

158
    Recognizes ever and anon
The breeze of Nature stirring in his soul.

          
The Excursion.
Book iv
.

159
    Pan himself,
The simple shepherd’s awe-inspiring god!

          
The Excursion.
Book iv
.

160
    I have seen
A curious child, who dwelt upon a tract
Of inland ground, applying to his ear
The convolutions of a smooth-lipped shell,
To which, in silence hushed, his very soul
Listened intensely; and his countenance soon
Brightened with joy, for from within were heard
Murmurings, whereby the monitor expressed
Mysterious union with his native sea.
 
13

          
The Excursion.
Book iv
